title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Restraint-Free Care & Least-Restrictive Safety
html:
The safest restraint is the one that can be avoided. Restraint and seclusion can cause physical and psychological harm and must never be used for convenience, discipline, coercion, retaliation, or routine fall prevention. The RN begins with the client’s behavior and underlying needs, uses individualized alternatives, and protects dignity and autonomy while responding to immediate danger.

Learning goals

  • Recognize when an intervention functions as a restraint.
  • Assess reversible causes of unsafe behavior before choosing an intervention.
  • Select individualized, least-restrictive alternatives.
  • Describe safe action when behavior creates immediate serious danger.
  • Apply order, monitoring, reassessment, documentation, and discontinuation principles.
  • Distinguish restraint from seclusion and from ordinary therapeutic care.

Define the intervention by its effect

A physical restraint is a manual method, device, material, or equipment that restricts a client’s movement or access to the body and that the client cannot easily remove. An item is not classified only by its name: side rails, a tightly positioned tray, or other equipment may function as a restraint depending on why and how it is used and whether the client can remove it. Equipment used in a standard way for an approved medical or surgical purpose may not be a restraint; follow current law, regulation, and policy.

A medication may function as a restraint when it is used to control behavior or restrict movement and is not a standard treatment or dosage for the client’s condition. Do not call an unnecessary sedating medication a “less restrictive” solution. Seclusion means involuntary confinement alone in an area the client is physically prevented from leaving and is limited to specific emergencies involving violent or self-destructive behavior under applicable rules.

Assess the cause before restricting movement

Describe exactly what the client is doing, when it began, and what risk is present. Look for pain, hypoxia, delirium, infection, medication effects, withdrawal, fear, communication barriers, hunger, thirst, toileting needs, sleep disruption, sensory impairment, unfamiliar surroundings, immobility, and equipment discomfort. Check whether the client understands the situation and can participate in a safety plan. A label such as “confused” is not an assessment and does not justify restraint.

Behavior is a cue, not the diagnosis
A client pulling at tubing may be hypoxic, in pain, frightened, delirious, or trying to toilet. Protect immediate safety while identifying and treating the cause. Restraining the hands without addressing the cause can worsen distress and risk.

Use individualized alternatives

Match alternatives to the reason for the behavior. Options may include calm reorientation, a qualified interpreter, hearing or vision aids, pain relief, toileting, hydration, sleep support, reduced noise, familiar objects, family or support-person presence when appropriate, purposeful activity, mobility assistance, closer observation, a room near staff, protection or repositioning of lines, and a tailored fall-prevention plan. Alarms or observation do not replace nursing assessment, and no single intervention is appropriate for every client.

Respond to immediate danger

When behavior presents an immediate serious danger to the client or others, summon help, reduce environmental hazards, use trained de-escalation and the least restrictive effective intervention, and follow the emergency response process. Staff safety matters; do not attempt a dangerous intervention alone. Restraint or seclusion is used only when required to protect immediate physical safety and less restrictive measures are ineffective or would be unsafe to attempt in that moment.

Authorization is time-limited—not permission to stop thinking

Obtain and renew the required order from the authorized practitioner within the applicable time frame. Standing or as-needed restraint orders are not acceptable under hospital restraint rules. Requirements differ by the type of restraint, behavior, age, setting, jurisdiction, and organizational policy. An order does not make restraint mandatory and does not permit continuing it after the unsafe situation ends.

Protect the client during use

Use only approved equipment, the correct size, trained technique, manufacturer instructions, and organizational policy. Maintain alignment and protect skin, circulation, breathing, and access to emergency care. Never obstruct an airway or use a position that compromises respiration. Preserve privacy and provide nutrition, hydration, elimination, hygiene, comfort, mobility or range of motion, communication, and medication assessment as appropriate.

Monitoring must be individualized and consistent with current rules and policy. Reassess behavior and the need for the intervention; respiratory and cardiovascular status; circulation and neurovascular findings; skin; mental status and distress; pain; hydration, nutrition, elimination, mobility, and readiness for release. Violent or self-destructive restraint or seclusion has additional evaluation and monitoring requirements. Obtain immediate help for breathing difficulty, altered perfusion, injury, escalating distress, or other deterioration.

Discontinue at the earliest possible time

Remove restraint or end seclusion as soon as the unsafe situation has resolved—even if time remains on the order. A trial release must never be used merely to restart or extend an expiring order. Continue the individualized safety plan, reassess the client and environment, and revise prevention strategies based on what was learned.

Document objective evidence

Record the specific behavior and immediate risk; assessment findings and likely contributors; alternatives attempted and the client’s response; the reason a more restrictive intervention became necessary; order and required notifications; type and location of the intervention; monitoring and care provided; injuries or changes; reassessments; criteria for release; time and response when discontinued; and education or debriefing as required. Documenting “restless” or “for safety” alone does not establish clinical necessity.

Clinical example

A hospitalized client with new confusion repeatedly tries to climb over the bedrail. The RN stays close, assists the client to safety, assesses oxygenation, pain, medication changes, toileting needs, infection cues, mobility, and sensory aids, and asks what the client is trying to do. After toileting and applying a tailored plan with frequent observation and assisted mobility, the behavior stops. Restraint is not added simply because the client has a fall-risk label.

Original educational synthesis. Restraint and seclusion requirements vary by setting and jurisdiction; follow current law, orders, organizational policy, manufacturer instructions, and qualified clinical instruction.
